Counting Triangles II

ParityCountingGraph Theory
Game: Count the little triangles by walking from one to the next, always to one that shares a side, and never to one you have already counted. How many can you reach?
How to play: Click a triangle to start, then click its neighbours one by one. Remove last takes a step back.
Look for the math

Lines parallel to the sides cut a triangle into n² small triangles. Walking from triangle to neighbouring triangle, you can never count them all. The best possible is

n² − n + 1

A chessboard of triangles

Paint the triangles that point up one colour and those that point down another (Show hint). Neighbours always have different colours, like the squares of a chessboard: it is a bipartite pattern. There are 1 + 2 + … + n = n(n+1)/2 up triangles but only n(n−1)/2 down ones.

Why the count is limited

A chain changes colour at every step, so it holds at most one more up triangle than down triangles: at most n(n−1)/2 + n(n−1)/2 + 1 = n² − n + 1 in all. That is a parity argument. The logic test searched every chain for n up to 5: the longest has exactly that length, and it begins and ends on an up triangle.

Reaching it

The bound can always be met. Snake through the rows, left to right and then right to left, and leave out one corner triangle in every row below the top: that skips n − 1 up triangles and counts all the rest. The test made this chain for every n from 2 to 16.

Start at the top triangle and snake down the rows. Which triangle must you give up in each row?
